extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (first-year math courses) writing solutions and proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and concrete style rules for composing readable, convincing mathematical solutions and proofs in undergraduate courses — how to structure equations, sentences, paragraphs, and justifications for a peer audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target audience / level of explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: For a first-year mathematics course, you should write with your peers as your target audience. This means that you should explain each of your deductions; you cannot include too much detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the amount of explanation based on the intended reader. In introductory courses assume peer-level knowledge and justify each deduction explicitly. Avoid omitting justifications that your intended reader would not immediately accept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Every argument has a thesis: this is the main point of your argument. Every other statement in your argument is aimed toward convincing the audience that the thesis statement is true. Usually, your thesis statement is determined by the question you are answering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the thesis (the claim to be proved) explicit or clearly implied by the problem statement, and organize all content toward demonstrating it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: phrases → sentences → paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Style is the relationship between the structure of the argument and its content. Phrases are the essay's content; the style is the way in which the phrases are connected to form sentences, the way in which the sentences are ordered to form paragraphs, and the organization of the paragraphs to form the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately assemble small algebraic or symbolic phrases into sentences that show logical connection; then group related sentences into paragraphs that cover single topics to mirror the argument's structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid listing isolated equations (make equations grammatical)
rubrics_metrics.description: An equation (or inequality) is a phrase: it has a subject (the left-hand side), a verb ('is', as in 'is equal to' or 'is less than'), and an object (the right-hand side). The example of a bare list of lines is not an essay — it is a list of phrases with no sentences or paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present isolated lines of algebra without words connecting them. Add punctuation and linking words so the reader can read the equations as parts of sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect phrases explicitly (use linking words)
rubrics_metrics.description: To construct an argument, we should join the phrases together so as to make the connection between them clear (e.g., using 'because', 'thus', 'since', or 'which implies').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert words like 'because', 'thus', 'therefore', 'so', or implication symbols with verbal explanation so each step's relation to the prior step is explicit. The guide shows transforming raw lines into '..., because ...' or into a chain using 'Thus' or '⇒'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical flow direction (write from known to conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The logical flow of the argument should flow in the same direction as the sentences; start with something that is clearly true, make a series of deductions, and end with the conclusion that the thesis statement is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order your steps so the reader is led forward from accepted truths toward the claim, not required to read backward to find the justification. Avoid presenting a claim that depends on later unestablished facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify non-trivial or domain-sensitive steps explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: If the justification for a phrase includes anything beyond the truth of the previous phrase, you must explicitly state that justification (for example, when simplifying expressions in a limit, note the theorem that permits replacing functions that agree off a point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using theorems, taking limits, cancelling factors where domain issues occur, or performing any step that is not immediate from the previous line, state the reason: e.g., 'since f(x)=g(x) for x≠a, lim f = lim g' or 'because a,b>0 so ab>0' to avoid hidden domain errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use transitional words correctly (avoid misuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'thus' and 'because' indicate that the following phrase is true because the preceding sentence is true. Use them only when that dependence actually holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not misuse 'thus' to assert facts that are not direct consequences of the preceding sentence. If additional hypotheses are required, state them rather than using a transitional word improperly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Each paragraph should be about a single topic. For longer questions you may require several paragraphs; plan them by subtopics (e.g., zeros/asymptotes, derivative, second derivative, then tie together).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize paragraphs so each handles one aspect of the argument or computation. This makes later summary and the final sketch/claim clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concluding paragraph for multi-paragraph solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: If your argument is complicated enough to merit more than one paragraph, you should end with a concluding paragraph which summarizes your results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conclusion should tie the parts together and state the final answer or sketch, as in the curve-sketching example where earlier paragraphs analyze components and the final paragraph presents the sketch.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the method when not specified and summarize complex methods
rubrics_metrics.description: If the method is not specified and you wish to use induction (or another named method), you should start your argument with a phrase similar to, 'We will prove the following statement using induction.' If the method you are using is complicated, you may wish to summarize the steps of your argument so that the reader knows what is going on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin solutions by declaring the chosen method when it's not dictated by the problem, and provide a roadmap for multi-step or nonstandard approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision checklist (readability and logical checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: After you have written your solution, re-read it and ask yourself: Is each paragraph about a single topic? Is each paragraph made up of complete, properly punctuated sentences? Does each phrase follow logically from the one before it? Is each logical leap justified? Does the progression from one phrase to the next match the argument you are trying to make?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these concrete questions as a rubric for self-evaluation before submission; they capture key stylistic and logical requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread by reading aloud
rubrics_metrics.description: Try reading your solution aloud. It is amazing how many errors and omissions you can catch simply by doing this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud reveals missing words, disconnected phrases, and unclear logical transitions that silent proofreading may miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish style from formatting and grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: Style is not a question of margin size, single- or double-spacing, or any other technical printing issue. This is formatting. Similarly, style is not grammar. Although related, it is possible to use good style even if you have difficulties with English grammar. Style is not separate from content, nor is it any less important. Your work will be graded on content and style together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the organization and clarity of the argument (style) rather than superficial formatting. Ensure content and style are integrated; good formatting alone does not substitute for clear argumentation.
